items.title: A problem whose scale is unknown
items.body: Dogs are being abandoned and found roaming Stockton's streets. Some are lost pets, some have been dumped, and others live with people experiencing homelessness. Their circumstances and needs differ.
paragraphs: Stockton Animal Services recorded 3,106 stray-dog intake events in 2024. In September 2026, Stockton Street Dogs reported encountering three to ten dumped dogs per week. These figures establish that dogs are entering the care system and being encountered by rescuers, but they do not tell us how many dogs currently need help or how many are going without care.
The scale of the unmet need remains unknown.

image.alt: Illustrative dog on a neighborhood sidewalk

items.title: Care exists, but access is limited
items.body: The municipal shelter faces recurring capacity pressure: emergencies take priority, while healthy strays require appointments. Affordable veterinary care is in high demand, and rescue organizations depend on donations, volunteers, and available foster homes.

items.title: A network of care providers
items.body: Stockton Animal Services handles municipal sheltering and animal-control calls; Stockton Street Dogs provides outreach, supplies, and rescue assistance; Hard Luck offers subsidized veterinary treatment; and St. Mary's Pathways provides transitional housing that accommodates pets. What each provider can offer at a given moment is not always clear.

items.title: Plans to expand care
items.body: Stockton is developing an animal shelter expansion costing roughly 10.47 million dollars and has authorized additional veterinary staffing and spay and neuter services. Stockton Street Dogs is proposing a Canine Campus for overflow and recovery. How much additional care these efforts will deliver remains to be established.

items.title: Reviewing the field-call records
items.body: Crossover received 7,183 Stockton Animal Services field-call records on November 2 and began reviewing them November 4. We are tracing requests and recorded responses. A call is not a count of unique dogs or of the street population.

image.alt: Illustrative records and notes on a desk

items.title: Firsthand work and outreach
items.body: Crossover visited Stockton Animal Services and applied to volunteer there. We also asked about Doggie Day Out and applied to volunteer with Stockton Street Dogs. Neither application establishes participation or completed onboarding.

items.title: Continue the records review
items.body: Document the calls' date range, definitions, missing information, and limits before drawing conclusions about response patterns or outcomes.

items.title: Follow up with care providers
items.body: Seek responses to the volunteer and Doggie Day Out inquiries, clarify current care pathways, and document what we learn.

items.title: How many dogs currently need help on Stockton's streets?
items.body: We also need to understand their circumstances and what help, if any, they need.

items.title: What happens when someone reports a dog?
items.body: The records may describe a response, but whether a dog ultimately received care remains to be established.

items.title: Where does access to care break down?
items.body: We still need to understand which services can accept a reported dog and which barriers people encounter when seeking help.
